reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive or relapsing symmetrical weakness and sensory loss affecting proximal and distal limbs, evolving over at least eight weeks
Reflexes are typically reduced or absent, and the tempo distinguishes it from the acute course of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Nerve conduction studies show features of demyelination such as conduction slowing, block, prolonged distal latencies, and dispersion
Cerebrospinal fluid usually shows raised protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation)
It is an immunotherapy-responsive disorder, with first-line options of corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange
Numerous mimics and variants exist, and testing for nodal-paranodal antibodies helps identify cases that respond poorly to standard therapy
Objective demonstration of treatment response supports the diagnosis and guides long-term maintenance
reference.pathophysiology: CIDP is an immune-mediated disorder in which cellular and humoral responses target components of peripheral nerve myelin and the nerve roots, producing segmental demyelination and secondary axonal loss. Repeated cycles of demyelination and attempted remyelination can lead to onion-bulb formation and nerve hypertrophy. The inflammatory process slows or blocks conduction, particularly at the roots and proximal segments, causing the characteristic weakness and sensory loss. A subgroup has antibodies against nodal or paranodal proteins such as neurofascin or contactin, defining a distinct autoimmune nodopathy with differing treatment response.
additionalDifferentials: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to demonstrate demyelinating features
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for albuminocytological dissociation
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein
MRI of nerve roots and plexuses to show hypertrophy or enhancement
Nerve biopsy in selected atypical cases
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory or bulbar involvement suggesting an acute or overlapping process
A monoclonal protein pointing to POEMS or a haematological disorder
Poor response to first-line therapy prompting reassessment and antibody testing
Prominent early axonal loss threatening irreversible disability
reference.prognosis: Most patients respond to immunotherapy and many achieve stable function or remission, but a proportion have relapsing or progressive disease with accumulating axonal loss and residual disability; early treatment improves outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing hereditary or paraprotein-associated neuropathy as CIDP
Relying on a single normal cerebrospinal fluid protein to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking nodal-paranodal antibody disease that responds poorly to intravenous immunoglobulin
Continuing ineffective therapy without objective evidence of response
